source.title: Enhancing Contrastive Learning with Noise-Guided Attack: Towards Continual Relation Extraction in the Wild
source.authors: Ting Wu; Jingyi Liu; Rui Zheng; Qi Zhang; Tao Gui; Xuanjing Huang

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied. Some table layout is flattened, but Table 1’s model, dataset, noise-rate, accuracy, and forgetting values can be assigned from its headers and ordering.
record.tranche_reason: The paper evaluates noisy-label learning in continual relation extraction, a new setting for the catalog claim, and reports test accuracy as label-noise rates vary. It does not measure fitting random labels to zero training error.
record.gate_note: The paper’s own Table 1 reports test accuracy for ten methods on two datasets at three noise rates; those results bear on noisy-label generalization (V4), but do not report training error or chance-level test error. Figures 6 and 9 show accuracy trends, but their values are figure-only and are not needed to represent the numerical Table 1 results. Table 2 memory-buffer purity and Table 3 attack/discard ablation results do not measure a listed claim version and are not rows. The paper’s discussion of learning simple patterns before noisy labels cites prior work.
record.test_reason: NaCL uses the premise that clean patterns are learned before noisy labels to select training samples. Its experiments evaluate noise mitigation through test accuracy, forgetting and sample selection; they do not establish random-label fitting or the temporal learning order named by the versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that existing continual relation extraction methods are vulnerable to label noise and that NaCL improves robustness and knowledge retention through clean-sample selection, noise-guided attack and memory replay.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains continual relation extraction models with synthetic label corruption and evaluates last-task test accuracy; it does not reproduce the original random-label fitting intervention. It uses BERT-based models and Adam in a continual learning setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and label-noise rate affect reported test accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 1 reports declining last test accuracy as corruption increases. For example, joint-training accuracy falls from 88.1% to 73.7% to 56.4% on FewRel; NaCL falls from 84.1% to 83.7% to 80.5%. These measurements do not establish fitting of corrupted training labels.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing label corruption reduces generalization performance in continual relation extraction, and NaCL generally improves robustness over the continual-learning baselines.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 3.2 reports that the loss separation between clean and noisy samples becomes less distinct across successive tasks; Figure 4 illustrates confidence-based sample selection after rebooting an auxiliary model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prior-task knowledge can impair loss-based clean-sample selection in continual relation extraction.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: No training accuracy is reported, so these results cannot establish whether the models fit corrupted training labels. The results concern continual relation extraction on two datasets and do not test the original random-label fitting claim. Accuracy is averaged over five random runs, but no error bars or confidence intervals are reported in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: No result rows retained: Table 1’s results concern test accuracy under noisy continual relation extraction and are recorded under fits_no_version because they do not measure training-set fitting or the specific behavior named by V4. Table 2 buffer purity, Table 3 ablation results, and Figures 6, 8, and 9 are outside the versions’ measured behaviors or are related measures only.

untested.parts: No completely random labeling experiment, training-error measurement, or chance-level test-error comparison.
No comparison of training time or convergence speed between true and random labels or across corruption fractions.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel or Gaussian-noise inputs.

Test accuracy declines across 10%, 30% and 50% corruption, but training-set fitting and noise memorization are not measured. The joint claim of perfect training fit with degradation toward chance is untested.
No experiments establish the necessity or sufficiency of weight decay, dropout or data augmentation.
The learning-order premise is used for sample selection. The supplied description of Figure 3 does not establish that clean patterns are learned before noisy labels are memorized.

record.verdict_notes: The record's tests/T3 classification conflicts with its empty rows and its explanation that the reported metrics do not measure training-set fitting. Test-accuracy degradation alone does not establish V4's coupled fitting-and-memorization behavior. The omitted tables and figures are already declared in rows_left_out.

versions.untested_parts: No experiment tests completely random labels, training error on them, or test error at chance.
No comparison of time or convergence speed for true versus random labels, or across corruption fractions.
No shuffled-pixel, permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

The paper varies random label corruption and reports test accuracy, but does not report training-set fit, perfect training accuracy, or whether remaining signal is learned while noise is memorized. The experiment is continual relation extraction, not the version’s stated general setting.
No tests of weight decay, dropout, data augmentation, or their removal.
No experiment measures whether real-label patterns are learned before noisy or random labels.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
